title: British Columbia Online Gambling 2026: PlayNow & What's Next
excerpt: How online gambling works in British Columbia in 2026, why PlayNow is the only regulated site, and whether BC will follow Ontario into an open market.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
British Columbia online gambling looks very different from the market taking shape in Ontario, and understanding that difference matters for any player on the west coast. While Ontario opened its doors to dozens of private operators, BC has kept a single, government-run model built around PlayNow.com. This guide explains how the province regulates online play in 2026, what PlayNow offers, and whether British Columbia might eventually follow Ontario toward a competitive market.

The BCLC monopoly model

Online gambling in British Columbia runs through the British Columbia Lottery Corporation, a Crown corporation that operates PlayNow.com as the province's only regulated online and mobile gambling site. Through PlayNow, residents can access lottery products, an eCasino with slots and table games, live-dealer tables, poker, bingo and a sportsbook, all under one government-run roof.

This is a fundamentally different approach from the open, multi-operator system in Ontario, where private brands compete for players under provincial licences. In BC, the province both runs the games and keeps the revenue, funnelling profits toward public services rather than private shareholders. Supporters argue the model keeps gambling proceeds within the province and maintains tight control over consumer protection. Critics counter that a monopoly offers less choice, fewer promotions and less innovation than a competitive market.

What single-event betting changed

The most significant shift for BC bettors came in 2021, when Canada legalised single-event sports betting through a change to the Criminal Code. Before that, bettors were limited to parlay-style wagers that required getting multiple outcomes right. Since the change, PlayNow has offered single-game betting on major leagues, bringing BC into line with the rest of the country on the core sports product.

That reform reshaped the sports side of the market, but it did not change the fundamental structure: PlayNow remained the only legal option. The grey market question

Because BC offers only one regulated site, many residents also play at offshore operators that accept Canadian customers. These international sites are not licensed by the province, and they operate in a legal grey area: it is not illegal for individuals to play at them, but they fall outside BCLC oversight and provincial consumer protections. Players who choose offshore sites take on more risk around dispute resolution, withdrawals and responsible-gambling safeguards.

This grey market is one of the central arguments in the debate over reform. Regulators in other provinces have pointed out that a large share of online gambling was already happening outside the government system, and that bringing those players into a licensed, taxed and regulated market improves safety while capturing revenue. That is precisely the logic Ontario used when it opened its market.

Could BC follow Ontario?

The Ontario experiment has become the reference point for every provincial gambling debate in Canada. Since launching its open market, Ontario has grown into the country's largest regulated online gambling jurisdiction, with online casino play now accounting for the overwhelming majority of its revenue and dozens of licensed operators competing for players. You can read our take on how that market matured in our coverage of Canada's evolving iGaming landscape.

For British Columbia, the question is whether the benefits of an open market outweigh the value of the current monopoly. Several factors are in play:

  • Revenue capture: an open, taxed market could pull grey-market players back into a regulated system and broaden the tax base.
  • Consumer protection: licensing private operators lets regulators enforce standards on advertising, responsible gambling and payouts.
  • Public revenue: the existing model already sends BCLC profits to provincial coffers, and any change would need to protect that funding.
  • Political appetite: opening a market is a major policy shift, and provinces move at their own pace based on local priorities.

As of 2026, British Columbia has not announced a move to an Ontario-style open market, and PlayNow remains the sole regulated option. But the direction of travel across Canada, combined with the proven Ontario template, keeps the conversation alive.

How BC compares with the rest of Canada

British Columbia is far from alone in running a government monopoly; most Canadian provinces still operate their online gambling through a single Crown corporation or lottery body. What makes the current moment interesting is that Ontario broke ranks and proved an open, private-operator market could work at scale, generating record volumes while maintaining regulatory oversight. Alberta has since signalled its own intent to move toward a competitive model, adding to the sense that the monopoly approach is no longer the only respectable path. British Columbia now sits among the provinces watching those experiments closely. Whether the province eventually opens up will likely depend on how the Ontario and Alberta markets perform on the measures that matter most to regulators: player safety, grey-market reduction and stable public revenue. For BC residents, the practical lesson is to stay informed, because the rules that govern their play could shift over the next few years.

What it means for BC players today

For now, the practical picture for British Columbia residents is straightforward. PlayNow is the only provincially regulated site, and it offers a full menu of casino, poker, bingo and sports products with the backing of provincial consumer protections. Players who value regulation and local oversight will find everything they need there.

Those who venture to offshore sites should do so with eyes open, prioritising operators with strong reputations, clear licensing from respected international regulators, and solid responsible-gambling tools. The bottom line

British Columbia in 2026 sits at an interesting crossroads. It has a stable, government-run system that many players trust, yet it looks increasingly conservative next to Ontario's booming open market. Whether BC eventually opens up or holds firm, the smart move for players is the same: understand the difference between regulated and offshore options, prioritise safety, and keep gambling firmly in the realm of entertainment.
